title: Industrial action is not one method

blocks.heading: Industrial action is not one method
blocks.text: Industrial action can take different forms. A strike stops work; picketing involves a protest presence outside the workplace; work to rule follows rules strictly in a way that slows operations; a go slow deliberately reduces working pace; non-cooperation refuses new working practices; an overtime ban refuses work beyond normal hours. A lock-out is an employer action excluding employees from the workplace. These are distinct mechanisms with different effects on output, earnings, service and relations. Describe the actual behaviour and who initiates it. The terms alone do not establish legality, entitlement or the correct procedure in a particular dispute. Disruption can create pressure to settle but also harms orders and trust, so it is not the same as resolving the underlying cause.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: At fictional Hena Works staff complete their normal hours but refuse extra evening hours. At another hypothetical workplace the employer shuts staff out during a dispute. The first is an overtime ban, not a strike stopping normal work. The second is a lock-out initiated by the employer, not an employee choosing to slow down.

blocks.heading: Strike
blocks.text: A strike is a form of industrial action where employees refuse to work. It withdraws labour to put pressure on the employer. It can interrupt output and customer service and can affect workers’ earnings and relations. This definition does not determine the legal status of a particular stoppage.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical group stops its normal work during a dispute. The stoppage is distinct from continuing to work slowly or refusing extra hours only.

blocks.heading: Picketing
blocks.text: Picketing involves employees taking action standing outside the workplace to protest at or seek to influence deliveries and the arrival or departure of others. It makes the dispute visible and seeks support or pressure. It is distinct from the act of stopping work itself; picketing may accompany a strike. Do not assume the term authorises intimidation or determines legal rights.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical group protests outside the gate during a dispute and asks others to support its position. The outside protest illustrates picketing; identify the stated behaviour rather than treating every protest as a different pay system.

blocks.heading: Work to rule
blocks.text: Work to rule is a form of industrial action when rules are strictly obeyed so that work is slowed down. Staff continue to work but withdraw informal flexibility, such as shortcuts or extra duties not required by the rules. It differs from deliberately reducing pace regardless of rules. Its effect depends on how ordinary work relies on that flexibility.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical team follows every required checking stage and refuses informal shortcuts during a dispute, slowing dispatch. The mechanism is strict rule compliance, not a complete stoppage.

blocks.heading: Go slow
blocks.text: A go slow is a form of industrial action when employees do their normal tasks but much slower than usual. Work continues, but deliberately reduced pace lowers output. It differs from work to rule, whose defining mechanism is strict compliance, and from a strike, which withdraws work. Slower supply can affect customers as well as the employer.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical production team deliberately reduces its working pace while continuing normal tasks. That is a go slow. The example does not state strict rule compliance as the reason for the slowdown.

blocks.heading: Non-cooperation
blocks.text: Non-cooperation is a form of industrial action when employees refuse to comply with new working practices. Staff may continue established duties while resisting a change. The defining feature is refusal of the new practice, not automatically refusing all work or every instruction. It can obstruct implementation while leaving existing operations partly active.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical team continues its old routine but refuses a proposed new scheduling method during a dispute. The refusal concerns a new practice, identifying non-cooperation rather than a general stoppage.

blocks.heading: Overtime ban
blocks.text: An overtime ban is a form of industrial action when employees refuse to work longer than their normal working hours. Normal contracted work continues, while extra hours are withdrawn. It can reduce output where the business relies on overtime. It differs from a strike stopping normal work and may have little production effect where no extra hours were needed.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical workshop’s staff complete their normal shift but refuse requested evening overtime. This is an overtime ban. Describing it as refusal to do normal work would change the stated action.

blocks.heading: Lock-out
blocks.text: In a lock-out employees are locked out of their workplace by the employer during a dispute. It is an employer action, unlike employees withdrawing labour in a strike. It can put pressure on employees but also stops operations and may damage relations and orders. The definition alone does not establish legal entitlement or procedure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A hypothetical employer excludes staff from the premises as pressure during a dispute. The employer initiates the exclusion, which distinguishes the lock-out from a strike or workers’ outside protest.
